{{Politics of Canada}}

The '''King's Privy Council for Canada''' ({{langx|fr|Conseil privé du Roi pour le Canada}}),{{#tag:ref|Referred to as the '''Queen's Privy Council for Canada''' ({{langx|fr|Conseil privé de la Reine pour le Canada}}) during the reign of a female monarch.<ref>{{citation| title=Official Report of Debates, House of Commons| volume=174| publisher=Queen's Printer| page=5237| year=1926}}</ref><ref>{{citation| title=Canadian Symbols of Authority: Maces, Chains, and Rods of Office| year=2011| publisher=Dundurn| last1=Pike| first1=Corinna| last2=McCreery| first2=Christopher |author-link2=Christopher McCreery | isbn=978-1-4597-0016-1| page=258}}</ref>|group=n|name=Queen}} sometimes called '''His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada'''{{#tag:ref|Referred to as the '''Her Majesty's Privy Council for Canada''' during the reign of a female monarch|group=n}} or simply the '''Privy Council''' ('''PC'''),<ref name=PCO>{{citation| url=http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/index.asp?lang=eng&page=information&sub=council-conseil&doc=facts-faits-eng.htm| author=Privy Council Office| author-link=Privy Council Office (Canada)| title=Queen's Privy Council for Canada – Facts| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=15 October 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606054719/http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/index.asp?lang=eng&page=information&sub=council-conseil&doc=facts-faits-eng.htm| archive-date=6 June 2011}}</ref> is the full group of personal advisors to the [[King of Canada]] on [[State (polity)|state]] and constitutional affairs. Practically, the tenets of [[responsible government]] require the sovereign or his [[viceroy]], the [[governor general of Canada|governor general]], almost always to follow only that [[Advice (constitutional)|advice]] tendered by the [[Cabinet of Canada|Cabinet]]: a committee within the Privy Council composed usually of elected [[members of Parliament]]. Those summoned to the Privy Council are appointed for life by the governor general on the advice of the [[prime minister of Canada|prime minister]]. The group is composed predominantly of former Cabinet ministers, with some others having been inducted as an honorary gesture. Privy counsellors are accorded the use of an honorific [[Style (manner of address)|style]] and [[post-nominal]] letters, as well as various signifiers of precedence.<ref name=appoint>{{cite web| url=http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/index.asp?lang=eng&page=information&sub=council-conseil&doc=members-membres/index-eng.htm| author=Privy Council Office| author-link=Privy Council Office (Canada)| title=Members of the Queen's Privy Council| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=15 October 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606054728/http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/index.asp?lang=eng&page=information&sub=council-conseil&doc=members-membres%2Findex-eng.htm| archive-date=6 June 2011}}</ref>

== {{Canadian monarch, current|title=1}}-in-Council ==
{{Further|Monarchy of Canada#Executive (King-in-Council)}}

The [[Government of Canada]], which is formally referred to as ''His Majesty's Government'',<ref>{{cite book| last=MacLeod| first=Kevin S.| author-link=Kevin S. MacLeod| title=A Crown of Maples| location=Ottawa| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| year=2015| page=18| url=https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/pch/documents/services/royal-symbols-titles/crnMpls-eng.pdf| isbn=978-0-662-46012-1| access-date=25 October 2015| archive-date=6 September 2017| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906040901/https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/pch/documents/services/royal-symbols-titles/crnMpls-eng.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| last=Wrong| first=Humphrey Hume| author-link=H. H. Wrong| contribution=Telegram 219| date=10 November 1952 |location=Ottawa| title=Relations With the United States | series=Documents on Canadian External Relations| volume=18-867| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120118010606/http://www.international.gc.ca/department/history-histoire/dcer/details-en.asp?intRefid=4363| contribution-url=http://www.international.gc.ca/department/history-histoire/dcer/details-en.asp?intRefid=4363| access-date=18 May 2009| archive-date=2012-01-18| publisher=[[Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade]]}}</ref> is defined by the [[Canadian constitution]] as the [[Monarchy of Canada|sovereign]] acting on the advice of the Privy Council;<ref>{{cite book| author=Her Majesty the Queen| author-link=Queen Victoria| publication-date=29 March 1867| title=Constitution Act, 1867| series=III.9| location=Westminster| publisher=Queen's Printer| url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/ca_1867.html |via=The Solon Law Archive | access-date=15 January 2009| year=1867}}</ref><ref name=Marleau>{{cite book| last1=Marleau| first1=Robert| author2=Montpetit, Camille| title=House of Commons Procedure and Practice| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| year=2000| location=Ottawa| id=1. Parliamentary Institutions > Institutional Framework > Executive| url=http://www2.parl.gc.ca/MarleauMontpetit/DocumentViewer.aspx?DocId=1001&Sec=Ch01&Seq=3&Lang=E| isbn=2-89461-378-4| access-date=2009-10-15| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008170948/http://www.parl.gc.ca/MarleauMontpetit/DocumentViewer.aspx?DocId=1001&Lang=E&Sec=Ch01&Seq=3| archive-date=2012-10-08}}</ref> what is known as the ''Governor-in-Council'',<ref>{{Cite book| last=Elizabeth II| author-link=Elizabeth II| date=1 April 2005| title=Interpretation Act| series=35.1| location=Ottawa| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| url=http://www.canlii.org/en/ca/laws/stat/rsc-1985-c-i-21/latest/rsc-1985-c-i-21.html| access-date=7 August 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090705082900/http://www.canlii.org/en/ca/laws/stat/rsc-1985-c-i-21/latest/rsc-1985-c-i-21.html| archive-date=July 5, 2009}}</ref> referring to the governor general of Canada as the {{Canadian monarch, current|title=1}}'s stand-in. The group of people is described as "a Council to aid and advise in the Government of Canada, to be styled the Queen's Privy Council for Canada",<ref name=BNA>{{Harvnb|Her Majesty the Queen| 1867| loc=III.11}}</ref> though, by [[Convention (norm)#Government|convention]], the task of giving the sovereign and governor general [[Advice (constitutional)|advice]] (in the construct of [[constitutional monarchy]] and [[responsible government]], this is typically binding{{#tag:ref|See [[Cabinet of Canada#Responsibilities|§ Responsibilities]] and the [[Cabinet of Canada#Royal prerogative against the prime minister|note]] at [[Cabinet of Canada]].|group=n|name=RP}}) on how to exercise the [[royal prerogative]] via [[Order in Council|orders-in-council]] rests with the Cabinet—a committee of the Privy Council made up of other [[Minister of the Crown|ministers of the Crown]] who are predominately drawn from, and are responsible to, the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]] in the [[Parliament of Canada|Parliament]].<ref name=Marleau /> This body is distinct but also entwined within the Privy Council, as the [[president of the King's Privy Council for Canada]] customarily serves as one of its members and Cabinet ministers receive assistance in the performance of their duties from the [[Privy Council Office (Canada)|Privy Council Office]], headed by the [[Clerk of the Privy Council (Canada)|clerk of the Privy Council]].

While the Cabinet specifically deals with the regular, day-to-day functions of the King-in-Council, occasions of wider national importance—such as the proclamation of a new Canadian sovereign following a [[demise of the Crown]] or conferring on royal marriages—will be attended to by more senior officials in the Privy Council, such as the prime minister, the [[Chief Justice of Canada|chief justice of Canada]], and other senior statesmen; though all privy councillors are invited to such meetings in theory, in practice, the composition of the gathering is determined by the prime minister of the day. The [[quorum]] for Privy Council meetings is four.<ref name=Palango>{{Cite news| last=Palango| first=Paul| title=Privy Council nod on royal betrothal 'medieval'| newspaper=Globe and Mail| date=8 May 1981}}</ref>

==Membership==
The ''[[Constitution Act, 1867]]'', outlines that persons are to be summoned and appointed for life to the King's Privy Council by the governor general,<ref name=BNA/> though convention dictates that this be done on the advice of the sitting prime minister. As its function is to provide the vehicle for advising the Crown, the members of the Privy Council are predominantly all living current and former ministers of the Crown. In addition, the chief justices of Canada and former governors general are appointed. From time to time, the [[Leader of the Opposition (Canada)|leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition]] and heads of other [[Opposition (parliamentary)|opposition]] parties will be appointed to the Privy Council, either as an honour or to facilitate the distribution of sensitive information under the ''[[Security of Information Act]]''. Similarly, it was required by law that the members of the [[Security Intelligence Review Committee]] be made privy councillors if they were not already, though this has not been required of the SIRC's successor since 2019, the [[National Security and Intelligence Review Agency]].

To date, only Prime Minister [[Paul Martin]] advised that [[Parliamentary Secretary|parliamentary secretaries]] be admitted to the Privy Council.
[[File:Swearing In - Assermentation (37356449481).jpg|thumb|[[Andrew Scheer]], then [[Leader of the Official Opposition (Canada)|leader of the opposition]], being sworn into the Privy Council at [[Rideau Hall]] in 2017]]

Appointees to the King's Privy Council must recite the requisite oath:<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.gg.ca/document.aspx?id=316| last=Office of the Governor General of Canada| author-link=Governor General of Canada| title=Oaths of Office| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=4 March 2007}}</ref>

{{blockquote|I, [name], do solemnly and sincerely swear (declare) that I shall be a true and faithful servant to His Majesty {{Canadian monarch, current|name&title=*}}, as a member of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada. I will in all things to be treated, debated and resolved in Privy Council, faithfully, honestly and truly declare my mind and my opinion. I shall keep secret all matters committed and revealed to me in this capacity, or that shall be secretly treated of in Council. Generally, in all things I shall do as a faithful and true servant ought to do for His Majesty.|author=|title=|source=}}

Provincial [[Premier (Canada)|premier]]s are not commonly appointed to the Privy Council, but have been made members on special occasions, such as the [[Canadian Centennial|centennial of Confederation]] in 1967 and the [[patriation]] of the constitution of Canada in 1982. On [[Canada Day]] in 1992, which also marked the 125th anniversary of [[Canadian Confederation]], Governor General [[Ramon Hnatyshyn]] appointed 18 prominent Canadians to the Privy Council, including the former Premier of Ontario [[David Peterson]], retired hockey star [[Maurice Richard]], and businessman [[Conrad Black]] (who was later expelled from the Privy Council by the Governor General on the advice of Prime Minister [[Stephen Harper]]<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/conrad-black-stripped-of-the-order-of-canada/article16644365/| title=Conrad Black stripped of the Order of Canada| date=31 January 2014| newspaper=Globe and Mail| access-date=24 April 2014}}</ref>). The use of Privy Council appointments as purely an honour was not employed again until 6 February 2006, when Harper advised the Governor General to appoint former member of Parliament [[John Reynolds (Canadian politician)|John Reynolds]], along with the [[28th Canadian Ministry|new Cabinet]]. Harper, on 15 October 2007, also advised Governor General [[Michaëlle Jean]] to appoint [[Jim Abbott (politician)|Jim Abbott]].
[[File:KingRoyals1927.jpg|thumb|left|[[Edward VIII|Prince Edward]] (front row, fifth from left), at [[Rideau Hall]], in [[Ottawa]], two days after being appointed to the King's Privy Council for Canada]]

Members of [[Monarchy of Canada#Royal family and house|the monarch's family]] have been appointed to the Privy Council: the Prince of Wales (Edward, later King [[Edward VIII]]), appointed during the reign of his father, King [[George V]], on 2 August 1927; [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]], appointed during the reign of his wife, Queen [[Elizabeth II]], on 14 October 1957; the Prince of Wales (Charles, now King [[Charles III]]), appointed during the reign of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, on 18 May 2014; and [[Queen Camilla]], appointed during the reign of her husband, King Charles III on 26 May 2025.<ref>{{citation| url=https://www.canada.ca/en/privy-council/services/queens.html#P| author=Government of Canada| title=King's Privy Council for Canada > Members of the King's Privy Council| date=11 December 2017| publisher=King's Printer for Canada| access-date=1 March 2023}}</ref><ref>{{citation| url=https://www.canada.ca/en/news/archive/2014/05/pm-announces-appointment-royal-highness-prince-wales-queen-privy-council-canada.html| author=Government of Canada| title=PM announces the appointment of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada| date=18 May 2014| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=1 March 2023}},</ref><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.thetimes.com/comment/register/article/court-circular-may-26-2025-fjxvccvqq| author=The Times| title=Court Circular: May 26, 2025| access-date= 27 May 2025}}</ref>

On occasion, non-Canadians have been appointed to the Privy Council. The first non-Canadian sworn of the council was [[Billy Hughes]], [[Prime Minister of Australia]], who was inducted on 18 February 1916, at the request of [[Robert Borden]]—to honour a visiting head of government, but also so that Hughes could attend Cabinet meetings on wartime policy.<ref>{{cite book| last=Fitzhardinge| first=Laurence| author-link=Laurie Fitzhardinge| date=1979| title=William Morris Hughes: A Political Biography / Vol. 2: The Little Digger, 1914–1952| publisher=[[Angus & Robertson]]| pages=71–72| isbn=0-207-13245-3}}</ref> Similarly, [[Winston Churchill]], [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom]], was inducted during a visit to Canada on 29 December 1941.<ref>{{cite news| title=Becomes Canadian Privy Councillor| url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2194&dat=19411230&id=UfcuAAAAIBAJ&pg=5272,5909124| newspaper=Ottawa Citizen| date=30 December 1941| access-date=3 May 2012}}</ref>

Privy councillors are entitled to the style ''[[the Honourable]]'' ({{langx|fr|L'honorable|link=no}}) or, for the prime minister, chief justice, or certain other eminent individuals, ''[[the Right Honourable]]'' ({{langx|fr|Le très honorable|link=no}}){{#tag:ref|When the style is held by a woman, the French title is: {{lang|fr|La très honorable}}.|group=n|name=Female}} and the [[post-nominal letters]] ''PC'' (in {{langx|fr|CP|links=no}}). Prior to 1967, the style ''the Right Honourable'' was only employed in Canada by those appointed to the [[Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council|Imperial Privy Council]] in [[London]], such persons usually being prime ministers, Supreme Court chief justices, certain senior members of the Canadian Cabinet, and other eminent Canadians. These appointments ended under [[Lester Pearson]], though the traditional style remained in use, limited to only prime ministers and chief justices. In 1992, several eminent privy councillors, most of whom were long-retired from active politics, were granted the style by the Governor General and, in 2002, [[Jean Chrétien]] recommended that [[Herb Gray]], a privy councillor of long standing, be given the style ''the Right Honourable'' upon his retirement from Parliament.<ref name=HerbGray>{{cite web| url=http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/default.asp?Language=E&Page=archivechretien&Sub=newsreleases&Doc=cabinet.20020115_e.htm| last=Privy Council Office| author-link=Privy Council Office (Canada)| title=Prime Minister Announces New Ministry| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=4 May 2008}}{{dead link|date=June 2023|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

==History==
According to [[Eugene Forsey]], Privy Council meetings—primarily meetings of the full Cabinet or the prime minister and senior ministers, held with the governor general presiding—were not infrequent occurrences in the first 15 years following [[Canadian Confederation]] in 1867.<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Forsey| first1=Eugene| title=Meetings of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, 1867-1882| journal=The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science|date=November 1966| volume=32| issue=4| pages=489–498| doi=10.2307/139891| jstor=139891}}</ref>  One example of a Privy Council meeting presided over by the governor general occurred on 15 August 1873, in which Governor General [[Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|the Earl of Dufferin]] outlined "the terms on which he would agree to a [[prorogation]] of Parliament" during the [[Pacific Scandal]].<ref>{{harvnb| Forsey| 1966| p=491}}</ref> When he served as viceroy, [[John Campbell, 9th Duke of Argyll|John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne]], put an end to the practice of the governor general presiding over Privy Council meetings, other than for ceremonial occasions.<ref>{{harvnb| Forsey| 1966| pp=489–498}}</ref>

Prime Minister [[William Lyon Mackenzie King]] had the Privy Council convene in 1947 to consent to [[Wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Philip Mountbatten|the marriage]] of Princess Elizabeth (later Queen [[Elizabeth II]]) to [[Philip Mountbatten]],<ref>{{citation| url=https://www.pressreader.com/canada/national-post-latest-edition/20220910/282063395805709| last=King| first=William L.M.| title=William Lyon Mackenzie King| date=10 September 2022| newspaper=National Post| via=[[PressReader]]| access-date=15 February 2023}}</ref> per the [[Royal Marriages Act 1772]]. The Princess' father, King [[George VI]], had offered an invitation for Mackenzie King to attend when the [[Privy Council of the United Kingdom]] met for the same purpose. But, the Prime Minister declined and held the meeting of the Canadian Privy Council so as to illustrate the separation between Canada's Crown and that of the UK.<ref name=Boyce81>{{cite book| last=Boyce| first=Peter John| title=The Queen's Other Realms: The Crown and Its Legacy in Australia, Canada and New Zealand| page=81| publisher=Federation Press| location=Sydney| year=2008| isbn=978-1-86287-700-9}}</ref>
[[File:Queen Elizabeth and members of the federal government of Canada in Ottawa 1957-10-14.jpg|thumb|The first meeting of the Privy Council before the reigning sovereign; in the State Dining Room of [[Rideau Hall]]. Queen [[Elizabeth II]] is seated at centre, with [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]], to her left, and Prime Minister [[John Diefenbaker]] at her right; 14 October 1957.]]

The Council has assembled in the presence of the sovereign on two occasions: The first was at 10:00&nbsp;a.m. on the [[Thanksgiving (Canada)|Thanksgiving Monday]] of 1957, at the monarch's residence in [[Ottawa]], [[Rideau Hall]]. There, Queen Elizabeth II chaired a meeting of 22 of her privy councilors, including her [[List of Canadian monarchs#LConsorts|consort]], by then titled as Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, who had just been appointed to the Privy Council at that same meeting. The Queen also approved an order-in-council.<ref name=Bousfield>{{cite book| last=Bousfield| first=Arthur|author2=Toffoli, Gary | title=Fifty Years the Queen| publisher=Dundurn Press| year=2002| location=Toronto| pages=11–12| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w8l5reK7NjoC| isbn=1-55002-360-8}}</ref><ref name=Buckner69>{{Cite book| last=Buckner| first=Phillip| publication-date=2005| contribution=The Last Great Royal Tour: Queen Elizabeth's 1959 Tour to Canada| editor-last=Buckner| editor-first=Phillip| title=Canada and the End of Empire| page=69| location=Vancouver| publisher=UBC Press| isbn=0-7748-0915-9| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=27IggObUC9kC| access-date=24 October 2009| year=2005}}</ref> Two years later, the Privy Council again met before the Queen, this time in [[Halifax, Nova Scotia]], to confirm the appointment of [[Georges Vanier]] as governor general.<ref name=PCO/><ref>{{Harvnb| Buckner| 2005| p=70}}</ref> There was originally some speculation that the coming together of the sovereign and her Council was not constitutionally sound. However, the Prime Minister at the time, [[John Diefenbaker]], found no legal impropriety in the idea and desired to create a physical illustration of Elizabeth's position of Queen of Canada being separate to that of Queen of the United Kingdom.<ref name=Bousfield/><ref name=Buckner69/>

A formal meeting of the Privy Council was held in 1981 to give formal consent to the marriage of Prince Charles, Prince of Wales (now King [[Charles III]]), to [[Diana, Princess of Wales|Lady Diana Spencer]].<ref name=Boyce81/> According to a contemporary newspaper account, the conference, on 27 March, at [[Rideau Hall]], consisted of 12 individuals, including Chief Justice [[Bora Laskin]], who presided over the meeting; Prime Minister [[Pierre Trudeau]]; several cabinet ministers; [[Stanley Knowles]] of the [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]]; and [[Alvin Hamilton]] of the [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative Party]].<ref name=Palango/> All gathered were informed of the Prince's engagement, nodded their approval, and then toasted the royal couple with [[Champagne (wine)|champagne]]. David Brown, an official in the Privy Council Office, told ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'' that, had the Privy Council rejected the Prince of Wales' engagement, none of his children would have been considered legitimate heirs to the [[Monarchy of Canada|Canadian throne]], thus setting up a potential break in the unified link to the crown of each of the [[Commonwealth realm]]s, in contradiction to the conventional "treaty" laid out in the preamble to the [[Statute of Westminster 1931|1931 Statute of Westminster]].<ref name=Palango/> Following the announcement of the Prince of Wales' engagement to [[Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall|Camilla Parker-Bowles]], however, the [[Department of Justice (Canada)|Department of Justice]] announced its conclusion that the Privy Council was not required to meet to give its approval to the marriage, as the union would not result in offspring that would impact the succession to the throne.<ref>{{Cite news| last=Valpy| first=Michael| author-link=Michael Valpy| title=Scholars scurry to find implications of royal wedding| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=2 November 2005| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/Page/document/v5/content/subscribe?user_URL=https://www.theglobeandmail.com%2Fservlet%2FArticleNews%2FTPStory%2FLAC%2F20050211%2FPROTOCOL11%2FTPInternational&ord=5357017&brand=theglobeandmail&force_login=true| access-date=4 March 2009}}</ref>

To mark the occasion of [[Ruby Jubilee of Elizabeth II|her Ruby Jubilee]], Queen Elizabeth II, on [[Canada Day]], 1992, presided over the swearing in of new members of her Privy Council.<ref>{{cite book| last1=Bousfield| first1=Arthur| last2=Toffoli| first2=Garry| title=Fifty Years the Queen: A Tribute to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II on Her Golden Jubilee| pages=200–201| publisher=Dundurn| location=Toronto| year=2002| isbn=978-1-55002-360-2}}</ref>

The most recent formal meeting of the Privy Council was on 10 September 2022, for the [[Proclamation of accession of Charles III#Canada|proclamation of the accession of King Charles III]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.gg.ca/en/media/news/2022/ceremony-proclaim-accession-king-charles-iii| author=Secretary to the Governor General of Canada| title=Ceremony to proclaim the Accession of the Sovereign to take place at Rideau Hall| publisher=King's Printer for Canada| date=9 September 2022| access-date=10 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| title=King Charles III proclaimed Canada's new head of state in ceremony at Rideau Hall| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-king-charles-ceremony-rideau-hall-canada/| access-date=10 September 2022| newspaper=Globe and Mail| agency=Canadian Press| date=10 September 2022}}</ref>
